title: Did Archibald James marry Elizabeth Breakey, and was little Archie their son?
desc: The narrator's central puzzle. The diary and Eliza Nelson's letters imply a marriage, but "there is no record of that marriage" {q:170} {q:T2:71}; the narrator says only that "there is no record at that date" (1823) {q:T2:68}, while affirming in both transcripts that Archibald "made the mistake of marrying that girl" {q:130} {q:T2:58}. That little Archie was the son of Archibald and Elizabeth Brakey is "believed, but not conclusively proven" {q:108} {q:T2:50}. A compiled genealogy adds a marriage of Archibald James Somerville to an Elizabeth Crawford on 30 November 1836, and a son Bellingham Brooke born in St Louis in 1852 {s:winters-p67} {s:winters-p68}; both details come from an online tree and the IGI and have not been checked. The narrator connects the question to the dormant baronetcy {q:174} {q:T2:73}. The second recording adds the narrator's fuller account: Archibald "got a family girl, a village girl from Monaghan named Brakey into the family way and subsequently married that girl. We can find no record of the marriage … only in family correspondence" {q:T3:132-133}; he "lived in Trinidad from … 1823 … till 1835", came home, and "in 1836 … married, in a church, somebody of his own class, a lady called Elizabeth Crawford", a marriage the narrator regards as bigamous because the first wife "was still alive at the time" {q:T3:133-135}. {ctx}The family's 1897 pedigree, sent in by Bellingham Arthur, records Archibald's birth at Kilkenny (13 May 1803) and death (7 February 1871), and neither marriage {s:visitation-1897}.
alternatives: Married to Elizabeth Brakey (perhaps irregularly or abroad); Archie legitimate
Not married to her; Archie acknowledged by his grandparents but illegitimate
The 1836 "Elizabeth Crawford" marriage is the same union, recorded later or under another surname
The 1836 marriage is to a different woman, a later family that settled in America
next: Church of Ireland and Presbyterian registers for Ballybay/Monaghan 1822–24; the original record behind the 1836 Crawford marriage; St Louis records for Bellingham Brooke Somerville; re-read the diary and the Nelson letters.

title: Who was the eighth son of Captain William and Eliza?
desc: "Eight boys and two girls" {q:84, 96} {q:T2:40}, but only seven sons are named in the recording. A compiled genealogy (quoting an Ancestry tree) lists an eighth: Tenison, born 10 and died 22 August 1812 {s:winters-p67}. {int}This fits the narrator's account of names being reused after a child died, since the next son was Tenison Alan (1815). Still needs a baptism or burial record. Resolved. The family's 1897 pedigree lists all ten children, eight of them sons: William Henry, Archibald James, John Churchill, Corry, Bellingham, Tenison (born at Newry 10 August, died 22 August 1812), Tenison Alan and Samuel Riall {s:visitation-1897}. The family Bible, as read in the second recording, has the same Tenison: "Tennyson born at Newry that's not Tennyson Allen that's Tennyson he died 12 days later" {q:T3:32}.
alternatives: Named in the Crisp's entry but not read out
The count of eight is a slip

title: Tenison or Tennyson?
desc: Both transcripts write "Tennyson" {q:14} {q:T2:7}, the speech-to-text default for the spoken name, so they are no evidence of the spelling. Eliza Bellingham's mother was Elizabeth Tenison and her brother Henry Tenison Bellingham {s:lf-bellingham}, and a compiled genealogy uses "Tenison Alan Somerville" throughout {s:winters-p67}. Tenison is very probably right; an original record would confirm it. Resolved: Tenison. The Times notice of Bellingham Arthur's death (1916) calls him the son of "the late Tenison Alan Somerville" (via {s:winters-p68}), and Cecil B. Rooke's papers file the family under "Tenison" {s:nli-rooke}.

title: When, and through whom, did Tenison get his Constabulary appointment?
desc: Tenison returned in 1840 {q:204} {q:T2:83}; the narrator credits Sir William Somerville as Chief Secretary {q:212-214} {q:T2:86-87}, but Sir William held that office only from July 1847 {s:wp-1st-baron}. A compiled genealogy records two of Tenison's sons baptised at St Paul's, Trinidad, in 1842 and 1845 {s:winters-p68}, which suggests he went back to the West Indies after his marriage ("they were always looking for appointments, particularly in the West Indies" {q:T2:83}) and joined the Constabulary later.
next: RIC/Irish Constabulary officer registers (National Archives UK, HO 184) for Tenison's date of appointment.

title: The other children of Tenison and Eliza O'Connor
desc: The narrator mentions only Bellingham Arthur and an unnamed elder brother, also in the RIC {q:12} {q:T2:6}, and then moves straight to Bellingham Arthur's own children {q:216-218} {q:T2:88}. A compiled genealogy citing the IGI lists six children: William Dennistoun (1842), Tenison Alan (1845–55), Erina Bellingham (1852), Bellingham Arthur (1853), Tenison Alan (1859) and Henry Bellingham (1859 or 1848) {s:winters-p68}. {int}The archive at first guessed that the elder brother in the RIC was William Dennistoun (see the resolution below). Audit, Oct 2026: the family tree dates Henry Bellingham Somerville's birth to 23 December 1848, not 1859; The Times's description of Bellingham Arthur as the fourth son favours 1848. It also records Erina as dying unmarried at Doncaster in 1927, against the compiled genealogy's 1883 marriage to Thomas Forster Woulfe {s:family-tree-2026}. Both conflicts are shown on the profiles. Resolved by the family's own pedigree, printed in 1897 {s:visitation-1897}: William Dennistoun (born Trinidad, 8 June 1842), Tenison Alan (Trinidad, 22 February 1845 – 13 April 1855), Henry Bellingham (Dublin, 23 December 1848; "an officer in the Royal Irish Constabulary"; married Mary Dyas 1880; one daughter, Elizabeth Mary), Erina Bellingham (Dublin, 30 July 1852; married 1883 the Rev. Thomas Forster Rolfe, not "Woulfe"), Bellingham Arthur (17 November 1853) and Tenison Alan (Dublin, 28 July 1859). There were no twins: the compiled genealogy's 1859 date for Henry is wrong. The "elder brother" in the RIC was therefore Henry, as the second recording confirms ("Bellingham Arthur's elder brother was called Henry Bellingham"; his daughter's confirmation of arms calls him "District Inspector, Royal Irish Constabulary") {q:T3:77} {q:T3:81}, not William Dennistoun, who, the narrator says, could not speak {q:T3:19-21}.
next: Optional: the RIC officers' register (HO 184) for Henry Bellingham Somerville.

title: Is the 1887 "District Inspector Somerville" Bellingham Arthur? (Resolved: yes)
desc: Hansard names only "District Inspector Somerville" (24 March 1887) and "Sub-Inspector Summerville" (10 May 1887) {s:hansard-1887} {s:hansard-1887c}; the local history gives no first name {s:ballymacoda-1887}. The family's story matches closely: an RIC detachment from Cork, a dead rioter named Hanlon, a blade, arrest, Parliament, and reinstatement without a formal acquittal {q:312-322} {q:T2:118-127}, which is just what the 10 May reply describes. The narrator remembered "the 1880s", "Captain" Somerville and a fishing dispute. {int}Resolved: the officer was Bellingham Arthur Somerville. The evidence: (1) he was a serving RIC officer of exactly that rank: he joined in 1872, aged 18, and was a "Retired D. I. R. I. Constabulary" at the 1891 census {s:winters-p68}; the rank had been renamed from sub-inspector in 1883, which explains the two titles {s:ukpga-1883-s12}. (2) Ronayne's letter shows the officer was a "young officer" from outside, not the local District Inspector, Kerin {s:hansard-1887b}, matching the family's detachment "from Cork". (3) The family's account, independent of Hansard, matches every structural point, including the outcome the 10 May reply describes. (4) The family links the affair to his transfer to Wicklow, after which his career soon ended. Limitations: no surviving document seen gives the officer's first name, and the RIC service register (HO 184) has not been examined; the identification is therefore circumstantial but strong, and would be overturned only if another RIC officer named Somerville were found serving in Co. Cork in 1887. {ctx}Audit, Oct 2026: the family's Ancestry tree places two of his children's births at Queenstown, Co. Cork, in 1884 and 1885 and a death there in December 1887, which would put him in east Cork throughout the Youghal affair {s:family-tree-2026}. The family's own 1897 pedigree confirms these births and the death "at Merville, Queenstown" {s:visitation-1897}. On 8 September 1887 the Attorney General told the Commons that a nolle prosequi had been entered at the Cork Assizes in "the Queen v. Sub-Inspector Somerville and Constable Ward" {s:hansard-1887-sep8}. In the second recording, the narrator's written profile of his grandfather, read with the interviewer, describes him as "arrested by D.I. Kellen of yore [Kerin of Youghal]" and "lodged in the county jail … with Constable Ward" {q:T3:163-164}.
next: Optional confirmation: RIC officers' register (National Archives UK, HO 184) for Bellingham Arthur Somerville's stations in 1887; Cork Examiner reports of the inquest.

title: Captain William's regiments
desc: Family tradition: South Cork Light Infantry, "allegedly", or perhaps North Cork; "searches have been made in the military records" without success {q:54-56} {q:T2:27-28}. His later militia regiment is clear in transcript B, "the Louth, that's the County Louth Militia" {q:T2:29}, where A garbles it {q:56}; a compiled genealogy agrees {s:winters-p67}. The regular regiment remains unconfirmed.
alternatives: South Cork Militia (light infantry)
North Cork Militia
A regular regiment of the line
next: Militia officer lists in the Army Lists c. 1795–1830.

title: Captain William: born 1776, 1777 or 1778?
desc: Narrator, first recording: 1777, "I think" {q:62} {q:T2:30}. Published genealogies: 1776 {s:lf-bellingham}; 3 March 1776 (Stirnet, quoted in a compiled genealogy) {s:winters-p67}; the family tree, 17 March. In the second recording the narrator read the family Bible's entry, heard as "born on the 7th of March, 1778" {q:T3:28}. Resolved: the family's own pedigree, printed in 1897 from the family's records, gives "born 7 March, bapt. at St. Thomas', Dublin, 11 March 1776" {s:visitation-1897}. The Bible's day agrees; its year, as heard, is probably a slip in the reading or the transcription, and the narrator's 1777 is a year out ({qn:q-family-bible}).
next: Optional: the St Thomas' baptism register, and a photograph of the Bible page.

title: Who was "Sir William Somerville the younger" at Ardrass?
desc: "Sir William Somerville the Younger inherited the house. Ardras? We don't know. I don't know. I suspect he did. Ardras continued, not in the possession of the Somerville family" {q:T2:44} {q:90}. It is unclear who "Sir William the Younger" is: perhaps a member of the senior (baronet) line, or a confusion with Captain William. The registered Somerville pedigree compiled by Cecil B. Rooke (G.O. MS 182A, 1955) should answer this {s:nli-rooke}.
next: Read G.O. MS 182A, pp. 119–130.

title: Who sold Castle Bellingham to Sir William: Alan or his widow?
desc: Narrator: Alan "sold it, actually, to his uncle" {q:36}. Published genealogy: Alan rented it to Sir William, and Monique sold the freehold by c. 1824, after Alan's death in 1821 {s:lf-bellingham}. Both agree that it passed to the uncle. Resolved in favour of the published genealogy: Alan first let Castle Bellingham to his uncle, and the freehold was sold by his widow Monique after his death in 1821, by about 1824 {s:lf-bellingham}. The narrator's "he sold it, actually, to his uncle" is right about the buyer, simplified about the seller.

title: The cousin in Canada who gave family members "a leg up"
desc: Transcript B clarifies A's garbled "regiment law for sale": "there was a cousin who was a regimental officer in Canada and he appears in the records as being, as giving a leg up to a number of family members" {q:T2:15-16} {q:30-34}; and "one of the Bellinghams was a descendant of an early settler in Canada" {q:T2:17}. The cousin is not identified. Monique's family, the Bâbys, were early settlers of Detroit, which may be what is meant. In the second recording the narrator calls the family tree of Corry Somerville's descendants "the Canadian family" {q:T3:177-178}, although Corry settled at Rochester, New York; whether this is connected with the cousin in Canada is not clear.

title: Was Dorothea or Eliza the eldest sister?
desc: Narrator: "Dorothea being Eliza's eldest sister" {q:144} {q:T2:63-64}. Published genealogy: Elizabeth b. 1779, Dorothea b. c. 1780, though Dorothea married first (1798) {s:lf-bellingham}. Resolved in the narrator's favour. The family Bible, as read in the second recording, calls Eliza "II[nd] daughter to Colonel Bellingham" {q:T3:28-29}, and the family's 1897 pedigree "Elizabeth, 2nd dau. of Colonel Henry Bellingham" {s:visitation-1897}; the narrator repeats that Dorothea was "the eldest of the three girls" {q:T3:236}. Dorothea's published birth year, c. 1780, is only an estimate.

title: Clonmel, and where Archibald took ship
desc: Transcript B settles the reading: he "spent a few days in Clonmel, and then taken ship" {q:T2:65}, where A has "include Mal" {q:148}. His aunt Dorothea Riall lived in Clonmel {s:lf-bellingham}. The port of embarkation (Clonmel is inland) is not stated.
alternatives: Waterford
Cork (Cove)

title: The house called "Farm"
desc: Transcript B: "another house called Farm, just called Farm, F-A-R-M, near Bell Turbot in County Cavan" {q:T2:77}; A garbles the place {q:182}. Belturbet, Co. Cavan is now secure; the house itself has not been located.
next: Griffith's Valuation and townland indexes around Belturbet.

title: Locate Cumry, Co. Monaghan
desc: Spelled out by the narrator as C-U-M-R-Y, which both transcripts preserve (B renders the word itself as "Cymru") {q:136} {q:T2:62}; near Ballybay {q:162} {q:T2:68}. Not yet found in townland indexes. Resolved: Cumry (Na Comraigh) is a townland in Aghnamullen parish, barony of Cremorne, near Ballybay {s:logainm-cumry}. The narrator's spelling is the official one. Which farm in the townland the family held is still unknown.
next: Griffith's Valuation (1858–60) and earlier tithe records for Cumry, to find the farm.

title: Tenison's Dublin address: "Livingston" or "Leinster" Avenue?
desc: Transcript A: "Livingston Avenue. Breath of Hines" {q:216}; transcript B: "Linster Avenue. Brathmines" {q:T2:87-88}. Leinster Road is in Rathmines {s:wp-rathmines}; Leinster Avenue is in North Strand, near the family's earlier home in Bayview Avenue {s:dublish-leinster-ave}. The family Bible, as read in the second recording, places Eliza's death in 1839 "at Bayview Avenue in the City of Dublin" {q:T3:29}, a few streets from Leinster Avenue.
alternatives: Leinster Road, Rathmines
Leinster Avenue, North Strand
Another street in Rathmines
next: Thom's Directory entries for T. A. Somerville, 1850–1895.

title: Bellingham Arthur's boyhood nickname
desc: Transcript B is clear: "As a boy, he was known as Fighting Atty. Atty being Arthur" {q:T2:12}; transcript A has "fighting atte" {q:24}. ("Artie" would sound the same.)

title: First name of the daughter who married Edmund Truell
desc: Vere. Transcript B names her three times ("Vere Demerly … the name Vere"; "Then the next sister, Vere. Vere married the second son") {q:T2:89-90} {q:T2:98}; A garbles the name as "there to money" {q:224}. A compiled genealogy citing The Times gives Vere Frances de Merlie Bellingham Somerville (1890–1976), married 14 August 1912 {s:winters-p68}.

title: Henry Rook or Rooke: surname and relationship
desc: Transcript B: "Henry Rook"; A: "Henry, Rock" and "Henry Oak" {q:232-234} {q:T2:94}. Both transcripts break the sentence as "who was actually her father. That's [Bellingham] Arthur's solicitor", which must mean her father's solicitor, since he was "years older" and her husband. Rook (or Rooke) is the likeliest surname. Resolved: Henry Rooke, solicitor, eldest son of Archdeacon Henry Rooke of Wicklow, married Cecilia Eliza Margaret Bellingham Somerville, daughter of Bellingham Arthur Somerville of Clermont, on 11 April 1912; he died in 1942 {s:nli-rooke}. He was her husband and her father's solicitor, never her father.

title: Aunt Eddie's husband: "Uncle John" or "Uncle Jordan"?
desc: Transcript A: "Uncle Jordan", "stationed in India for that part of his career" {q:256-260}; transcript B: "Uncle John", "stationed in India for the whole of his career … years older than Eddie" {q:T2:102-103}. A compiled genealogy notes a 1929 Times notice for Edeline {s:winters-p68}, perhaps her marriage.
next: The Times, 1929; Army Lists (Royal Engineers).

title: Who commanded at Archangel, and in which regiment? (Resolved: Bunt, King's Own)
desc: Narrator: Bunt, "in the Royal Lancaster Regiment", commanded a troop sent to Archangel {q:364} {q:T2:144-145}; Jim was "a gunner, Royal Artillery" {q:366} {q:T2:145}. A war-diary-based history: "Lt. Col. W A T B Somerville DSO (Royal Artillery)" commanded the 8th (Special) Battalion MGC from 12 April 1919 {s:mgc-8bn}. A compiled genealogy citing The Times: Bunt a Lieutenant Colonel of the King's Own; Jim "Lieutenant Colonel, DSO, Royal Artillery" {s:winters-p68} {s:winters-p69}. Either the published commander's initials or his regiment and DSO are wrong, or Bunt transferred. Resolved: the commander at Archangel was Bunt, and his regiment was the King's Own (Royal Lancaster), as the narrator said. The initials W. A. T. B. are his alone; The Times (via a compiled genealogy) makes him a Lieutenant Colonel of the King's Own {s:winters-p69}; King's Own sources (seen in search results) name him as adjutant of the 1st Battalion and as "Captain W A T Somerville DSO" {s:kingsown-1914}. The battalion history's "(Royal Artillery)" is judged a confusion with his brother Jim. Still unconfirmed: the date and citation of Bunt's DSO, and whether Jim also held one.
next: The London Gazette for Bunt's DSO; the King's Own regimental history.

title: Pat's capture, escapes and camps
desc: Narrator: captured "in the retreat from Mons"; escaped three times, the third successfully, across Germany and Holland; MC {q:442-450} {q:T2:170-173}. The family has camp photographs and an "article" about the escape {q:452} {q:T2:173-175}. Other accounts: Captain Gualter Somerville, 2nd Bn Royal Warwickshire Regiment, Ströhen camp, nine escape attempts (TheGenealogist, search results) {s:genealogist-pow}; captured at Zonnebeke near Ypres in October 1914, escaped 1917 (an article based on interviews with the narrator) {s:clarke-sense-of-duty}; MC 1919 (IWM, search results) {s:iwm-gualter}. The 2nd Battalion arrived only in October 1914 {s:wp-royal-warwick}. Partly resolved: the archive now follows the records on place and date. Prisoner-of-war records and an article drawing on his debriefing report place his capture at Zonnebeke, near Ypres, in October 1914, with the 2nd Battalion, which reached Belgium only that month and was never at Mons. The narrator's "retreat from Mons" is kept as his recollection. Still to confirm from the originals: the number of escapes (three in the family account, nine in the records), the camps, and the MC entry in the London Gazette.
next: National Archives (UK) WO 339 officer file; ICRC 1914–18 prisoner archive; London Gazette 1919 MC entry; the family's article and photographs.

title: "Gunners Venture" in Kenya
desc: "A company called Gunner's Venture … started by Gunner officers after the First World War who wanted a job" {q:T2:193} {q:498-500}. No independent record found yet under that name. Partly resolved: the company existed. A scholarly article on Nanyuki in the 1920s (seen only in search results) describes Gunners' Venture Limited as a farm of about 17,000 acres near Nanyuki, with a sawmill, owned by ex-artillery officers {s:paice-nanyuki}, just as the narrator described it ("started by Gunner officers after the First World War"). Reginald's role there, and whether it grew coffee, are unconfirmed.
next: Read the article directly; Kenya Gazette company notices.

title: "Green desert" near Bantry
desc: Both transcripts hear "Green desert" {q:374} {q:T2:147}. A compiled genealogy citing The Times gives Bunt's death at Reendesert Lodge, Bantry {s:winters-p69}, so the place is evidently Reendesert. Still to check: the Times notice itself and the house's location. Resolved: Reendesert Lodge, Bantry. Both Bunt's death notice and Alan Ferguson's (The Times, via a compiled genealogy) name it {s:winters-p69}; it was the Fergusons' home before Kitty married Bunt.

title: Where is Uncle Jim buried?
desc: Transcript B: "he's buried in Rathnew" {q:T2:151}; transcript A: "buried in Matthew" {q:388}. Rathnew is the likelier reading; the grave has not been located. Audit, Oct 2026: his death was registered in Rathdrum district (family tree), which includes Rathnew and Clermont, as transcript B's "buried in Rathnew" implies.
next: Rathnew (Church of Ireland) burial register, 1950.

title: When was Clermont sold?
desc: "By the time it was all finished, it was about 1950", followed by a fragment both transcripts garble: "253" (A) and "2.53" (B) {q:566} {q:T2:224-225}. Perhaps "'52, '53", but that is a reading, not a fact. A heritage summary gives c. 1955 and the religious order came in 1956 {s:wicklowheritage-clermont} {s:irishaesthete-clermont}.

title: Was Kitty Harrison previously married to Alan Ferguson?
desc: "She married, or she had married, an Australian called Alan Ferguson" {q:374} {q:T2:146-147}. A compiled genealogy citing The Times confirms a marriage to Alan Campbell Ferguson before 1920 and to Bunt about 1925 {s:winters-p69}. Whether Ferguson died or the marriage ended in divorce is not recorded. Resolved: Alan Campbell Ferguson died on 21 September 1920 at Seaview, Isle of Wight, so Kitty was his widow; Reendesert Lodge was among his residences (The Times, via a compiled genealogy) {s:winters-p69}.

title: The Johnson ancestry
desc: From the interviewer's Ancestry tree, read aloud: Honor's father Philip (the Rector of Wicklow), whom the narrator confirms ("Philip was my grandfather" {q:T2:203}); his father Samuel Johnson, also confirmed {q:T2:203}; then "Zachariah" or "Samuel the Elder", and a Frances Tench, both unconfirmed {q:520-524} {q:T2:203-206}. Audit, Oct 2026: the family tree as exported now gives Rev. Phillip Bernard Johnson (1866–1926) ← Samuel Johnson (1812–83) ← William Abraham Johnson (c. 1775–1829) and Frances Tench ← Zacharias Johnson; the repeated "Samuel" the interviewer saw are probably Frances Tench's father and grandfather, both Samuel Tench {s:family-tree-2026}. The archive now follows this structure, labelled as unverified family information; apart from the 1911 census, none of it is sourced.
next: Clergy of Dublin and Glendalough succession lists for the Rectors of Wicklow; Church of Ireland records.

title: "William P. … William J." in the online tree
desc: The interviewer reads out entries ("William Henry, son of William J … I have William P, who is father of William J. William P being William Padlew") {q:118-120} {q:T2:53} that cannot be matched to anyone in the narrator's account. Resolved (audit, Oct 2026): the names come from the interviewer's own Ancestry tree, which labels Major William (1720–80) "William Padlou Somerville" and Captain William "William James Somerville" {s:family-tree-2026}. "William Henry, son of William J" is Captain William's son. The middle names Padlou and James appear in no other source (Stirnet, Burke, Wikipedia) and are not adopted.

title: Whose deaths prompted the destruction of the diary?
desc: Both transcripts agree on the wording: "following the death of my great-grandparents, that's my Aunt Eddie's parents, the end of the 19th century" {q:134} {q:T2:60-61}. So this is a slip in the testimony, not a transcription error. Eddie's parents died in 1916 and 1949; the narrator's great-grandparents (Tenison and Eliza, Eddie's grandparents) died around 1890–95 {q:T2:88}. We read "parents" as "grandparents".

title: Date of the recording
desc: Transcript A's file is labelled "27 Oct at 16-17"; transcript B's file is stamped "2026-10-27 19.50.34". The narrator, born 1937, is "coming up to 90" {q:50} {q:T2:25}. Everything points to 27 October 2026, but file timestamps record when the files were made, not necessarily the conversation. Resolved as far as the evidence allows: the speakers are now identified as William Somerville and his grandson Gergely (family information), both transcript files are stamped 27 October 2026, and nothing in the recording contradicts that date, so it is adopted. A second conversation (transcript C) was recorded the next day: its file is named "28", and the narrator refers back to what he "mentioned yesterday" {q:T3:8} {q:T3:17}. It is dated 28 October 2026.

title: Where are the original papers?
desc: The recording refers to Bellingham Arthur's six volumes {q:6} {q:T2:3}; his office and personal diaries, which the narrator owns {q:T2:133}; transcripts of Captain William's diary {q:132} {q:T2:59-60}; Eliza's letter about Henry {q:52} {q:T2:25-26}; the Nelson correspondence {q:166} {q:T2:69}; the Crisp's entry {q:124} {q:T2:54-55}; portraits of Dorothea and Monique and a miniature of Henry {q:26-28} {q:36} {q:44} {q:T2:13} {q:T2:18} {q:T2:22}; Pat's camp photographs and an article about his escape {q:452} {q:T2:173-175}; Reginald's Kenya photographs {q:504} {q:T2:196}; and Monique's booklet {q:42} {q:T2:21}. Cousin Eliza began photographing the portraits {q:46} {q:T2:23}. An inventory, with scans linked from this archive, is the most valuable next step. Partly resolved: some of the papers can now be located. (1) Cecil B. Rooke's own Somerville research (notebooks, will and parish-register extracts partly copied by Bellingham Arthur, letters from her brother Reg and sister-in-law Vere, the supporting notes for the 1955 pedigree) is in the National Library of Ireland's Rooke Papers, Ms. 33,584–33,601. (2) The registered Somerville pedigree is G.O. MS 182A, pp. 119–130, at the National Library. (3) In 1998 the library noted that "The Somerville Papers are now in the possession of Mr. William Somerville", the narrator {s:nli-rooke}. An inventory of what the narrator holds is still the most valuable next step. The second recording (transcript C) shows much of what the narrator holds: the family Bible, with an envelope containing a page of Captain William's original record, Tenison Alan's copy of 1850 and his record of his own children {q:T3:25-34}; Bellingham Arthur's notebooks {q:T3:4-11}; the family's copy of the Visitation of Ireland, with handwritten additions {q:T3:13-24}; Lily Somerville's confirmation of arms of 1924, with its seal {q:T3:76-87}; a 1929 newspaper cutting {q:T3:88-96}; the sales brochure of Somerville House {q:T3:101}; the pedigree rolls of the 1950s and a family tree of Corry's descendants {q:T3:177-188}; "three volumes of the history of the Somervilles", bought by Reginald at auction (probably The Memorie of the Somervilles, published in 1815 {s:wp-lord-somerville}) {q:T3:255-256}; and the portraits and miniatures at the other house {q:T3:236-275}. The interviewer photographed many of them {q:T3:12} {q:T3:14} {q:T3:87} {q:T3:96} {q:T3:233}, and the narrator's typed profiles were copied to him {q:T3:150-175} {q:T3:193-194}.
next: Transcribe the interviewer's photographs of the Bible pages, the confirmation of arms and the cutting; inventory and scan the rest; consult G.O. MS 182A and the Grants and Confirmations register, vol. M.

title: "For 19 years": the family's time in Monaghan, or Archibald's age?
desc: Transcript B: "At the time, Captain William and Eliza were living in County Monaghan for 19 years" {q:T2:51}. Transcript A: "At the time. Captain, William and Eliza. Were living. About 19 years. Archibald James. And, Next brother" {q:110-112}, which could mean Archibald was about 19 (as he was in 1823 {q:T2:9}). Without the audio, both readings remain.

title: Whose servant was Elizabeth Brakey?
desc: Transcript A: "a servant girl in some household" {q:110}; transcript B: "a servant girl in the Somerville household" {q:T2:51}. The difference matters to how the family story is told, and only the audio could settle it.

title: When did Tenison Alan Somerville die, and who died first?
desc: Transcript B: "they lived there until he died first. I think about 1890. Early 1890s. She died about 1895" {q:T2:88}; A is garbled ("about 189…") {q:216}. A compiled genealogy gives Tenison's death as 31 July 1895 {s:winters-p67} and none for his wife. Either the narrator's order of deaths or the online date is wrong. Partly resolved: the archive adopts 31 July 1895 (IGI, via the compiled genealogy) for Tenison's death, rather than the narrator's "about 1890". Whether he or his wife died first is still open, since no record of her death has been found. Audit, Oct 2026: the family tree gives Eliza (Cecilia Eliza Priscilla) O'Connor's death as 31 December 1898 at Rathmines {s:family-tree-2026}. If right, the narrator's order (Tenison first) is correct and both his dates are early. Uncited. The family's 1897 pedigree confirms 31 July 1895, with his burial in Mount Jerome Cemetery on 3 August and probate of his will on 20 September 1895 {s:visitation-1897}; the date is now secure. Whether his wife died after him remains open.
next: Civil death register, Rathmines, December 1898 (for Eliza).

title: Bellingham Arthur's birth: 1853 or 1856?
desc: Narrator: "born in 18… It's the year of the Crimean War, anyway. I think it was 1856" {q:T2:1-2} {q:2}. IGI, via a compiled genealogy: born 17 November 1853, baptised in Dublin 16 June 1854 {s:winters-p68}. The Crimean War (1853–56) fits both years. Resolved in favour of the records: 17 November 1853. A baptism in June 1854 rules out 1856, and his RIC enlistment age (18 in 1872) and 1891 census age (36) agree with 1853 {s:winters-p68}. The narrator's "1856" is kept as his recollection; the Crimean War, which he used to date it, began in 1853.

title: Rachel: Margaret's sister or her mother?
desc: The narrator: Margaret's elder sister and co-heiress was "Rachel" {q:330} {q:T2:131}. A compiled genealogy names Margaret's mother as Rachel Hall Wright {s:winters-p68}. Both could be true. Partly resolved: the 1891 census at Witney lists Margaret's mother as Rachel H. Clinch, aged 64, with her husband William Clinch (70, banker and brewer) {s:winters-p68}. So a Rachel Clinch certainly existed in the right household: Margaret's mother. Whether Margaret also had a sister Rachel who shared the inheritance, as the narrator says, is unconfirmed; he may have conflated mother and sister. Audit, Oct 2026: the family tree records only Margaret as a child of William Clinch and Rachel Hall Wright, and dates their deaths to 1891 and 1894 {s:family-tree-2026}; William Clinch's will (probate 1891) would settle the inheritance. The family's 1897 pedigree calls Margaret "2nd dau. of William Clinch of The Elms, Witney, by Rachel Hall his wife, dau. of John Wright" {s:visitation-1897}: her mother was Rachel, and there was an elder daughter, which supports the narrator's account of a sister who shared the inheritance, though the pedigree does not name her.
next: Probate calendar and will of William Clinch of Witney, 1891.

title: Where was Reginald's Kenya farm?
desc: "Eventually his mother bought a farm … a thatched hut … he built it up"; transcript B adds "a long way from Nanyuki" {q:T2:196-197}, where A has "Long way from UK" {q:504}.

title: Maudie Moore: "from Greystokes"?
desc: Transcript B: "he married a girl from Greystokes called Maudie Moore. She came from the County Laois family" {q:T2:197}; A: "grace studs … Morde Moore … County leash family" {q:506-508}. Greystones, Co. Wicklow is a guess, and her formal first name is not recorded. Audit, Oct 2026: the family tree names her father Arthur Ellard Hawkesworth Moore and gives her birth as January 1901 (uncited) {s:family-tree-2026}; the NLI list of the Rooke Papers records a 1946 letter from Reg Somerville referring to "the Ellard family" {s:nli-rooke}. A lead only.
next: The 1928 marriage record (Ireland or Kenya); Kenya Gazette notices.

title: What killed Bellingham Arthur in 1916?
desc: "He died, unfortunately, in 1916 of the flu that was then going around in the First World War"; asked if it was the Spanish flu, the narrator says "I always thought that he died of the Spanish flu, but … was that just after the First World War?" {q:10-12} {q:T2:4-5}. The 1918–19 pandemic came later {s:dcc-flu}, so it was not the Spanish flu as usually dated. What illness it was (influenza or something else) is unconfirmed. A compiled genealogy gives the date of death as 20 January 1916 {s:winters-p68}.
next: The civil death certificate (Rathnew/Wicklow registration district, January 1916).

title: Who, if anyone, is heir to the dormant Somerville baronetcy?
desc: The baronetcy became dormant when the 2nd Baron Athlumney, the 6th Baronet, died childless on 8 January 1929 {q:174} {q:T2:73} {s:wp-2nd-baron} {s:wp-somerville-baronets}; the press then reported that "Major William A.T.B. Somerville" (Bunt) was "heir to the baronetcy" {q:T3:92-93}. The narrator's family claim it as the senior surviving male line from Major William, second son of the 1st Baronet. His father "started to make" the claim in the 1950s–60s, and he is now pursuing it with the College of Arms, where the pursuivant handling it "was optimistic" {q:T3:71-72} {q:T3:139-140} {q:T3:188-189}. This archive does not decide the claim; it sets out the evidence for each branch. (1) The senior line, from Quaile, ended in 1929 {s:wp-somerville-baronets}. (2) Major William's only son was Captain William {s:visitation-1897}. (3) Captain William's eldest son, William Henry, "died s.p. in 1847", without children {s:visitation-1897}. (4) Archibald James, the second son, is the crux. The narrator holds that he married Elizabeth Brakey about 1823, that his 1836 church marriage to Elizabeth Crawford was therefore bigamous, and that the "American Somervilles" descended from it are illegitimate {q:T3:132-136} {q:T3:142-144}. But there is "no record of the marriage … only in family correspondence" {q:T3:132-133}, and the family's own 1897 pedigree records no marriage or children for him {s:visitation-1897}. {int}The argument cuts both ways: if the first marriage cannot be proved, the second cannot be shown to be bigamous, and the Crawford line (Bellingham Brooke Somerville, born at St Louis in 1852 {s:winters-p68}) would rank first; if it can be proved, and little Archie was born in wedlock and left sons, his line would rank first instead ({qn:q-archibald-marriage}). (5) Corry, the fourth son: the narrator found that he married Lucinda in Dublin, and that his only son, William Bellingham Somerville, died childless {q:T3:178-181} ({qn:q-corry-line}). (6) John Churchill, Tenison and Samuel Riall died as infants, and Bellingham (1810–44) left no recorded children {s:visitation-1897}. (7) Tenison Alan, the seventh son: his eldest son William Dennistoun is not known to have married; Tenison Alan (1845) died a child; Henry Bellingham had only a daughter, Lily {q:T3:77} {s:visitation-1897}; then comes Bellingham Arthur, whose younger brother Tenison Alan (1859) ranks after him. Of Bellingham Arthur's sons, Bunt, Jim and Pat had no sons, the narrator says, so the line passes to Reginald, the youngest, and to the narrator {q:T3:72}. After him: "If I die, James is the next heir … Then it goes to Charles" {q:T3:73}. In the latest Debrett's, on the advice of a professional genealogist, an American descendant ("John Somerville in Texas") is described as "probably" the baronet {q:T3:131} {q:T3:137}. The narrator calls him the sixth baronet; since the 2nd Baron was the 6th, a successor would be the 7th {s:wp-somerville-baronets}. To be recognised, a claim must be proved for entry on the Official Roll of the Baronetage {s:wp-official-roll}.
alternatives: The narrator's line (Tenison Alan, Bellingham Arthur, Reginald) is senior, if Archibald James left no legitimate male line and William Dennistoun had no sons
Archibald James's American descendants by Elizabeth Crawford are senior, if no earlier marriage can be proved
Little Archie's line is senior, if Archibald married Elizabeth Brakey before his birth and the line continued
next: The College of Arms file (Rouge Dragon Pursuivant); the latest and penultimate editions of Debrett's; William Dennistoun Somerville's marriage, if any; the 1836 Crawford marriage record and Bellingham Brooke Somerville's descendants; the Dublin marriage of Corry and Lucinda (about 1834).

title: Reginald's birth year
desc: Both transcripts: "My father was 17 when the Great War started in 1914" {q:348} {q:T2:138}, and "He was 38 at the time" (about 1934) {q:510} {q:T2:199}. Those imply 1896–97, but no record has been found. Audit, Oct 2026: the family tree cites a civil birth registration in 1897, Rathdrum district (which includes Clermont), and the 1901 and 1911 censuses {s:family-tree-2026}. 1897 is adopted as probable. Resolved: the printed additions to the family's pedigree record "Reginald Malcolm John Bellingham Somerville, born at Clermont 14 February 1897" {s:visitation-additions}, and in the second recording the narrator reads the same date from the family's copy, where his father had written in his own entry {q:T3:14} {q:T3:24}.

title: The Hungarian family: the gulag story
desc: Not Somerville history, but part of the recording. Near the end the interviewer, Gergely Somerville, describes his mother's side of the family: a mother who is the last authority on it, a grandfather Miklós, and a great-grandmother who died about 2010 in a flat in Eger, Hungary. She "always told these stories about her husband … him being sent to a gulag, and apparently escaping", but "no one really knows if the story was true" {q:588-598} {q:T2:235-240}. It is recorded here as her story, as Gergely reported it; nothing in it has been checked. Audit note: the family's Ancestry tree identifies the people concerned; as they belong to a separate branch of the family, their names are not published here.
next: Family papers and relatives' recollections, to establish the great-grandfather's name and the approximate date; with those, Hungarian archives.

title: The family Bible: what exactly does it record?
desc: The narrator keeps the family Bible in which Captain William "entered in all his ten children here … As they were born or baptized" {q:T3:26-27}, with an envelope holding a page of the original record, Tenison Alan's copy of 1850 and his record of his own children {q:T3:34}. In the second recording he read some entries aloud {q:T3:28-32}. Most agree with the family's printed pedigree of 1897 {s:visitation-1897}: Captain William's day of birth (7 March), the marriage on 30 August 1800, Eliza as "2nd daughter", the first Eliza's birth on 1 February 1808, and births at Lucan, Newry and Dundalk. Three dates, as heard, do not: Captain William's year ("1778"; the pedigree has 1776), Eliza's birth ("the 8th of September 1772"; the pedigree has 5 September 1779, and her parents married only in June 1772) and her death ("the 18th of December 1839"; the pedigree has the 16th). The Bible also has the first Eliza dying "at Warren Point … on the 13th of June, 1812" {q:T3:31}, where the pedigree has 13 January ({qn:q-eliza-infant-death}). {int}With only one machine transcript, a misheard number cannot be told from a misread one; and the 1897 pedigree may itself follow Tenison Alan's 1850 copy rather than the original page. The interviewer photographed pages as they talked {q:T3:27}; a transcription from the photographs would settle these points.
alternatives: The transcript misheard the numbers
The narrator misread the handwriting
The Bible and the 1897 pedigree genuinely differ (the pedigree may follow Tenison Alan's copy)
next: Transcribe the Bible pages and the 1850 copy from the interviewer's photographs, and compare them with the 1897 pedigree.

title: The confirmation of arms: when, and on what evidence?
desc: The narrator: "In our case, our family's case, there wasn't a formal grant of arms, but there was a confirmation of arms", obtained by Lily Somerville "in the 1930s, I think it was" {q:T3:76-78}. He read the original aloud: Sir Nevile Wilkinson, Ulster King of Arms, confirms to "Elizabeth Mary Somerville … only child of Henry Bellingham Somerville" and to "the descendants of the Major Somerville in His Majesty's Army" arms "long used and borne" by the family but not recorded {q:T3:80-85}. Partly resolved: the National Library's catalogue of the Genealogical Office register ("Grants and Confirmations of Arms", vol. M, 1920–29, fol. 44) dates the confirmation 2 April 1924 {s:nli-arms-1924}, a description known here only from search results. The arms are those printed with the family's pedigree in 1897, where, unlike the next pedigree in the volume, they are not described as "on record in the Ulster Office" {s:visitation-1897}. Open: what evidence of use was submitted, and whether the 1924 grant adds a mark of difference for Major William's line.
next: Read vol. M, fol. 44, at the National Library, and the date on the original letters patent.

title: Corry Somerville's marriage and descendants
desc: Corry matters to the baronetcy because he was older than Tenison Alan. In the first recording the narrator spoke of his illegitimate children and of his marriage to Lucinda, who had worked in the household {q:126-130} {q:178-180} {q:T2:56} {q:T2:75-76}. In the second he reports his own recent research: "I found … that he did marry Lucinda. And so all his children were legitimate. He only had one son, William Bellingham Somerville. And he died without any children. So the male line of Corrie died with him"; "Corrie and Lucinda were married in Dublin before they went west to America … to Rochester and New York"; the rest of the family "consisted of daughters" {q:T3:178-181}. The question was first raised by the Garter King of Arms in the 1950s or 1960s {q:T3:180}. {ctx}A compiled genealogy dates the marriage to 16 May 1834 and Corry's death to 12 January 1880 at Cleveland, Ohio {s:winters-p67}; the family's 1897 pedigree has "died in America 20 January 1879" and records no marriage or children {s:visitation-1897}. Partly resolved: the narrator's finding removes Corry's line from the succession if the son's death without issue is documented.
next: The Dublin marriage record (about 1834); Corry's death record (1879 or 1880); William Bellingham Somerville's death; the family tree of Corry's descendants in the narrator's keeping.

title: Was Eliza Bellingham's mother the granddaughter of Judge Tennison?
desc: Showing a portrait, the narrator says: "That is Judge Tennyson. And his granddaughter was the mother of Eliza Bellingham" {q:T3:274}. Eliza's mother, Elizabeth Tenison (c. 1750–1814), was "dau. of Richard Tenison of Thomastown, co. Louth" {s:visitation-1897} {s:lf-bellingham}. {ctx}Thomas Tennison (1707–1779), MP for Dunleer and a judge of the Common Pleas, had "one son, Richard, who predeceased his father by 20 years, leaving at least one daughter but no son" {s:wp-thomas-tennison}. {int}Partly resolved: a Richard Tenison of Co. Louth who died about 1759 leaving a daughter fits Elizabeth well, and supports the narrator; but no document seen names the daughter. It also corrects the family's online tree, which had made her the daughter of a Richard Tenison who died in 1725.
next: Judge Tennison's will (1779) or his son Richard's; Kingsley's sources for Elizabeth Tenison.

title: Who was "Wicked Alan"?
desc: A portrait at the family house is labelled on the back, as read aloud, "Wicked Alan, son of Henry Bellingham" and "probably" {q:T3:273-274}. {ctx}Two Alans were sons of a Henry Bellingham: {p:alan-bellingham-1709|Alan} (1709–96), son of Henry Bellingham, MP for Dundalk, and {p:alan-bellingham-1773|Alan} (c. 1773–1821), son of Lt-Col. Henry, whom the narrator described as "unsuccessful" and "unstable" and who lost Castle Bellingham {q:28-30} {s:lf-bellingham}. Kingsley calls neither of them wicked. A third, Alan Bellingham (1656–93) of the English Levens line, was "an ingenious but unhappy young man" who ran up debts {s:lf-bellingham}.
alternatives: Alan Bellingham (c. 1773–1821), Eliza's brother
Alan Bellingham (1709–96), Eliza's grandfather
next: Examine the portrait's label and costume; family letters mentioning "Wicked Alan".

title: When and where did the first Eliza die?
desc: The family Bible, as read aloud: "February 1st, 1808 … died at Warren Point near Newry on landing from Liverpool on the 13th of June, 1812, buried in Clonallan churchyard" {q:T3:31}. The 1897 pedigree: born at Athboy 1 February 1808, "died 13 January 1812" {s:visitation-1897}. A compiled genealogy: 13 June 1812 {s:winters-p67}. {int}June fits the family's movements: her brother Tenison was born at Newry, a few miles from Warrenpoint, that August {s:visitation-1897}.
next: Clonallan burial register, 1812.

title: Who is the Quentin Somerville of "the Quentin Somerville debacle"?
desc: In the first recording the interviewer asked about "the Quentin Somerville debacle"; the narrator said only "He's not a Somerville at all … Not in our line, at least" {q:176} {q:T2:74}. Resolved by the second recording and the published record: Sir Quentin Agnew-Somerville (1929–2010), son of Sir Peter Agnew and Enid Boan, who under the will of his uncle by marriage, the 2nd Baron Athlumney, inherited the Somerville estate in Co. Meath and took the name Somerville in 1950 {q:T3:110-116} {s:wp-agnew-somerville}. The "debacle" is presumably the loss of Somerville to a family that "wasn't even an illegitimate Somerville" {q:T3:112}, and its later sale.

title: Which Bellingham was given the freedom of Dublin?
desc: Reading the family's pedigree, the narrator says "Bellingham also got the freedom of the city of Dublin", and adds that it could be had by descent {q:T3:17-18}. Resolved: the 1897 pedigree records four admissions to the Freedom of the City of Dublin: Captain William and his son Bellingham on 10 January 1842, Tenison Alan on 18 July 1883 and Bellingham Arthur on 19 May 1893 {s:visitation-1897}.
